pages.title: The Ahî Organization
pages.content:
The Ahî Organization, which emerged in 13th-century Anatolia, was a religious and social institution that subsequently played a crucial role in the establishment of the Ottoman Empire. Throughout the centuries, the institution guided society with principles and rules governing moral, sociocultural, and commercial life. The word ‘Ahî’ is derived either from the Arabic word ‘ah’, meaning ‘brother’, or from the Turkish word ‘akı’, meaning ‘generous and brave’. In the Arabic reading, ‘ahî’ means ‘my brother.’

To fully grasp the function of the Ahî organization, we must first focus on fütüvvet organizations, which heavily influenced the establishment of the Ahî organizations in Anatolia.

pages.title: The Fütüvvet Tradition
pages.content:
Fütüvvet is a social concept that emerged during the first century of Islam, rooted in the term ‘fetâ’ from the pre-Islamic period. In pre-Islamic Arab society, the term ‘fetâ’ referred to qualities like generosity, bravery, fearlessness, helpfulness, and virtue. By the 9th century, the concept developed into a structured movement organizing young people socially, economically, and politically. Also in the 9th century, as the Sufi movement expanded from an individual lifestyle into an organized form, fütüvvet adopted a ‘Sufi fütüvvet’ identity and became a part of Sufism. Later, during the late Abbasid period in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, it became an official state organization. In its final stage, it became integrated with the artisan class, functioning as a professional organization while mostly keeping its Sufi character.

The concept of fütüvvet reached Anatolia through the Abbasids. From the 13th century onwards, it acquired a unique meaning among Anatolian Turks and turned into the Ahî movement.

pages.title: The Caliph’s Robe
pages.content:
Indeed, during the reign of Sultan Alâeddin Keykubad I (1220–1237), the Abbasid Caliph Nâsır-Lidînillâh (1180–1225), who regarded himself as the leader of the fütüvvet order, sent a fütüvvet robe to the sultan through an emissary. The envoy sent by the caliph was Şehâbeddin es-Sühreverdî (d. 1234). Nasir-Lidinillah aimed to rule the entire Islamic world, not just in theory but also in practice, and Sühreverdî acted as a key advisor in line with this goal. Being a well-known mufassir, hadith scholar, and beloved Sufi, Sühreverdî had the influence needed to unite scattered fütüvvet groups and restructure them for this purpose.

To this end, the Caliph intended to grant official status to the fütüvvet institution, which had previously been unofficial. By transforming the organization into a governmental body, he sought to give it legitimacy and secure its political support. Consequently, this institution, which had long been an independent force during times of weak central authority, would be brought under state control. While carrying out this important task, the Caliph relied heavily on Sühreverdî, benefiting greatly from his immense spiritual influence and strategic ideas. Upon his arrival in Konya, Sühreverdî was received with great ceremony and dressed Alaeddin Keykubad in the ceremonial robe sent by the Caliph. Through this act, the Abbasid Caliph officially recognized Keykubad’s political authority.

pages.title: Ahî Evran and the Spread of the Ahîs
pages.content:
On the other hand, Ahî Evran, who played a crucial role in the establishment of the Ahî order in Anatolia, gained the support of the Seljuk rulers. Ahî Evran was a Sufi mystic, a versatile scholar, and a philosopher who traveled to Anatolia from Central Asia. He stayed in Denizli, Konya, and Kayseri for a time, and visited many other cities and towns before finally settling in Kırşehir. Known as the spiritual leader of tanners and other craftsmen, Ahî Evran established a zaviye in Kırşehir that became the socio-religious and professional center for artisans all across Anatolia.

The members of this organization spread rapidly throughout Anatolia. The order extended from major cities to rural villages, reaching city dwellers as well as nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples. In 13th-century Anatolia, a period when state authority was severely weakened, the Ahîs played an important role in urban life, both economically and politically. They demonstrated their political and military power during times when central authority broke down and anarchy emerged. In fact, during the Mongol invasion, Ahî units took control of city administrations as local authorities.

The Ahîs resisted Gıyâseddin II, suspecting him of the assassination of Alaeddin Keykubad I. Alaeddin Keykubad I had faithfully supported the Ahî order and is believed to have been poisoned by his son. Later, following Gıyâseddin II’s defeat by the Mongols at Kösedağ, the Ahîs took part in the defense of Kayseri against the Mongols, who had already seized Tokat and Sivas, although the city eventually fell.

pages.title: Values and Way of Life
pages.content:
Rooted in Islamic-Sufi thought and the principles of fütüvvet, the Ahî Organization was closely linked to tekkes and zaviyes. It also shaped economic life by regulating the relationships between masters, journeymen, and apprentices in their workshops. For example, during the Anatolian Seljuk era, this order functioned like a system of trade guilds. In this role, it was responsible for resolving trade-specific issues and managing relations with the state. Additionally, enforcing quality control and regulating prices were among the primary duties of the order.

Their values, beliefs, and way of life from the 13th to the 16th centuries were recorded in the Fütüvvetnameler (handbooks of the organization). Through these texts, Ahî traditions shared a deep connection with the cultural education of the Alevi-Bektashi community and other groups in Anatolia.

The Fütüvvet way of life includes several key characteristics that guide a person’s behavior. Followers are expected to be generous, honest, and grateful, while always showing a cheerful face and speaking with kind words. They should help their families, treat workers well, and share meals with others. Furthermore, it is crucial to avoid bad company and instead seek the company of wise elders. Finally, followers must stay away from actions forbidden by the Qur’an and the Sunnah, such as consuming alcohol, and remember that this world is temporary. They must also support fellow believers by exchanging gifts and making donations.

pages.title: Education in the Ahî Organization
pages.content:
Role models play a crucial role in Ahî education, helping people develop good behavior and receive vocational training. The Fütüvvetnameler describe the qualities that these role models must possess in great detail, including performing the five daily prayers, remaining modest, and avoiding worldly attachments tied to self-interest. They must also stay away from what Allah has forbidden, obey His commands, earn a halal livelihood, and generously support their brothers in faith with kindness, while promoting good and forbidding evil.

In general, seeking knowledge is a fundamental requirement of the Ahî organization. Members are expected to form close ties with scholars and seek guidance from experts. If individuals lack the skills needed for their profession, they must actively learn them from a master or an educated person, and they must deeply value that knowledge. According to traditional Ahî teachings, failing to learn a craft properly brings shame both in this world and in the afterlife. Therefore, one must never attempt a task without proper training. Ultimately, the activities within fütüvvet circles were, in essence, a form of education.

People who began their Ahî training at a young age went through specific ranks and examinations. They started as apprentices, advanced to journeymen, and eventually became masters. The goal of these stages was to help individuals integrate what they had learned into their daily behavior. In a sense, every aspect of a zaviye member’s life was under supervision. The rules governing all their actions, from walking down the street to visiting the sick, were taught through reading, oral instructions, or the example of a role model.

Alongside the madrasas (established in Anatolia after the arrival of the Turks) and the Sufi tekkes that provided public education, Ahî zaviyes were also widespread educational institutions with a very broad sphere of influence. These zaviyes functioned as a type of school and played a significant role in educating the people of Anatolia. Their education covered every aspect of life. These institutions shaped society’s worldview and functioned as cultural centers where Anatolian Turkish society flourished.

pages.title: The Ahîs and the Ottoman State
pages.content:
The Ahî movement also played a major role in the founding of the Ottoman Empire. Historical sources mention the Ahîs, who were originally part of Turkmen groups, as one of the four groups that took an active part in establishing the empire. It is known that most of the early Ottoman sultans and viziers were connected with the Ahî organization. For instance, Murad I joined this organization, and it was used as a military force during conquests. However, especially beginning in the reign of Mehmed II (1444–1446, 1451–1481), the Ahî institution lost its political power. From that period on, it became an organization that only managed the administrative affairs of craft guilds.

In conclusion, the organization carried out important tasks not only in the field of education but also in the economic, military, and political spheres. Indeed, the 14th-century traveler from Tangier, Ibn Battuta, explained that the Ahî organization was found nowhere else. He noted that all the world’s beauties were found together in one place in Anatolia. The text attributes this to the brotherhood, which transformed the region into a highly prosperous area with exceptional social, economic, and political order.

pages.title: Joining Ceremonies
pages.content:
Initiation into the Ahî organization involved ceremonial practices such as drinking şerbet and dressing members in a traditional belt, peştamal, or şalvar. These rituals held symbolic significance. For instance, the act of wearing the traditional belt represented the following:

The belt has seven names, and each name carries one principle. The belt has seven principles. It carries seven specific meanings for both tying and untying, with each symbolizing a different virtue.

Here, doors are opened for good deeds and closed to bad ones, thus welcoming righteous actions while strictly avoiding wrongdoing.

That is to say:

Close the door of stinginess and open the door of generosity,

Close the door of anger and open the door of patience,

Close the door of greed and desire and open the door of contentment,

Close the door of overindulgence and worldly pleasures and open the door of self-discipline and repentance,

Close the door to worldly expectations from other people and open the door to the gifts of the Creator,

Close the door to idleness and idle talk and open the door to knowledge and wisdom,

Close the door of evil deeds and open the door of righteous deeds.

exercises.title: Notice: Degrees of Certainty
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: presented as established fact, or as belief?
exercises.question: How certain is the writer?

items: It is known that most of the early Ottoman sultans and viziers were connected with the Ahî organization.
The concept of fütüvvet reached Anatolia through the Abbasids.
Alaeddin Keykubad I … is believed to have been poisoned by his son.

Established fact: It is known that most of the early Ottoman sultans and viziers were connected with the Ahî organization.
The concept of fütüvvet reached Anatolia through the Abbasids.
Belief: Alaeddin Keykubad I … is believed to have been poisoned by his son.

exercises.explanation: The writer distinguishes “It is known that” (established) from “is believed to have been” (less certain) (Chapters 4 and 7).

feedback.correct: Good. You noticed the degrees of certainty.
feedback.incorrect: Compare known and believed.

exercises.title: Notice: Participle Clauses
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences. Then choose the one where the participle clause gives a reason.
exercises.question: Which participle clause gives a reason?
options: Being a well-known mufassir, Sühreverdî had the influence needed to unite scattered groups.
Rooted in Islamic-Sufi thought, the Ahî Organization was linked to tekkes.
Fütüvvet became integrated with the artisan class, functioning as a professional organization.
exercises.explanation: “Being …” at the start can give a reason (= because he was). “Rooted in …” gives background, and “functioning as …” describes a simultaneous action.

feedback.correct: Correct. Being … gives a reason.
feedback.incorrect: Which one can be rewritten with because?

exercises.title: Notice: Which After a Comma
exercises.instructions: Read the statement. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: In a non-defining relative clause between commas, we can use that instead of which.
exercises.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (between commas) use which or who, not that: “The Ahî Organization, which emerged in 13th-century Anatolia, …”.

feedback.correct: Correct. We use which, not that.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the first sentence of the book.

exercises.title: Use: Ethics and Work Today
exercises.instructions: Write an argument of eight to ten sentences: can modern workplaces learn from the Ahî tradition?
exercises.question: What should they learn, and what are the limits?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Modern workplaces can learn a great deal from the Ahî tradition. Rooted in the idea of brotherhood, the Ahî order connected skill with character. Members were expected to be honest and to treat workers well, and the order enforced quality control and regulated prices. Furthermore, young people advanced from apprentice to master under careful supervision. Today, many companies focus on profit and speed. However, not every Ahî rule fits a modern, diverse workplace, and some practices belonged to their own time. Nevertheless, the core values of honesty, fairness and learning from experienced colleagues are still relevant. Ultimately, a workplace that combines skill and ethics earns both success and trust.”

feedback.correct: Check: a clear claim, evidence from two chapters, a counterpoint and a conclusion.
